title: Announcing Ray support for PyTorch on Google TPUs | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale and Google Cloud launched native Ray support for PyTorch on Google TPUs via TorchTPU and KubeRay on GKE, replacing the JAX-style one-worker-per-host model with one worker per chip so GPU PyTorch code ports by swapping 'cuda'/'nccl' for 'tpu'/'tpu_dist'. Ray Train and Ray Serve/vLLM now run on topology-aware TPU slices with the same APIs as GPUs, framed as extending the PARK stack and lowering CUDA lock-in.

themes.theme: Google TPUs open to PyTorch via Ray

insights.claim: Anyscale and Google Cloud announced native Ray support for PyTorch on Google TPUs, built on Google's TorchTPU backend and KubeRay on GKE.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: Google is actively courting the PyTorch/GPU-native developer base, a direct attempt to erode CUDA lock-in for TPU adoption.
insights.quote: Today Anyscale and Google Cloud are announcing native Ray support for PyTorch on Google TPUs
insights.locator: Today Anyscale and Google Cloud are announcing

insights.claim: Before this integration, TPU workloads on Ray had to use a JAX-oriented SPMD model where one Ray worker per host VM managed all attached TPU chips, unlike the one-worker-per-device model PyTorch developers use on GPUs.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: The JAX-centric execution model was a structural adoption barrier for TPUs among PyTorch shops; removing it widens TPU's addressable market.
insights.quote: a Single-Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) execution model designed primarily for JAX

insights.claim: Ray now runs one worker per TPU chip, with each worker requesting resources={"TPU": 1} analogous to num_gpus=1, and isolates chips via TPU_VISIBLE_CHIPS the way CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES works for GPUs.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: Mirroring GPU abstractions one-to-one lowers TPU switching cost to near-zero at the orchestration layer.

insights.claim: According to the authors, migrating existing PyTorch code inside a Ray task from GPUs to TPUs requires only changing the device string from "cuda" to "tpu" and the collectives backend from "nccl" to "tpu_dist".
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: If true in practice, accelerator choice becomes a pricing/availability decision rather than a code-rewrite decision, pressuring Nvidia's software moat.
insights.quote: migrating existing PyTorch code from GPUs to TPUs is as simple as changing "cuda" to "tpu"

insights.claim: Ray's SlicePlacementGroup API gang-schedules actors onto the same multi-host TPU slice, which GKE provisions as node pools linked over high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI).
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: Interconnect topology, not chip count, is becoming the scheduling unit, favoring orchestrators that understand physical layout.

insights.claim: Ray Train's TorchTrainer, configured with use_tpu=True plus a topology (e.g. "4x4") and accelerator_type (TPU-V6E or TPU-V7X), atomically reserves contiguous TPU slices to prevent resource fragmentation.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: Fragmentation of scarce accelerator capacity is a real cost driver; atomic slice reservation improves utilization economics.
insights.quote: guarantees that all training workers are gang-scheduled onto contiguous physical TPU slices over high-speed ICI, preventing resource fragmentation

themes.theme: Zero-change training and serving on TPU

insights.claim: Existing Ray Train TorchTrainer scripts using DDP, FSDPv2 or DTensor can run on single- and multi-host Cloud TPU slices with zero changes to the PyTorch training loop, with Ray auto-configuring RANK, WORLD_SIZE and the tpu_dist process group.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: Removes the main engineering tax of trying TPUs for training, making multi-vendor accelerator procurement more credible.
insights.quote: with zero changes to your PyTorch training loop

insights.claim: The article's reference example scales a PyTorch training loop across a 16-chip multi-host Trillium (TPU-V6E, 4x4 topology) slice.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: Showcased configurations are modest-scale, suggesting the integration targets mainstream enterprise workloads first rather than frontier-scale runs.
insights.locator: Here is a complete example of scaling

insights.claim: vLLM-TorchTPU registers TorchTPU as a vLLM platform plugin so PyTorch models run on Cloud TPUs without rewriting them in JAX, and Ray Serve LLM deploys OpenAI-compatible endpoints on TPU slices via the same LLMConfig API used on GPUs.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: TPU inference becomes a drop-in alternative to H100 serving, intensifying price competition in the inference market.
insights.quote: PyTorch models compile and execute on Cloud TPUs without rewriting model definitions in JAX

insights.claim: The serving example deploys google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it on a TPU-V6E 4x4 slice with tensor_parallel_size 16 and expert parallelism enabled, with the only GPU-vs-TPU difference being accelerator_type H100 vs TPU-V6E.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: Google uses its own MoE Gemma model as the showcase, positioning TPU as a direct H100 substitute for MoE inference.

themes.theme: PARK stack as open AI standard

insights.claim: Anyscale argues the PARK stack (PyTorch, AI models, Ray, Kubernetes) is becoming the industry standard for production AI as workloads evolve into compound systems combining training, high-throughput inference and reinforcement learning.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: Anyscale is positioning Ray as the default orchestration layer across accelerators, a hardware-neutral control point worth tracking as AI infra consolidates.
insights.quote: organizations are standardizing on the open-source PARK stack (PyTorch, AI models, Ray, and Kubernetes)
insights.locator: Extending the PARK stack to TPUs

insights.claim: The integration lets platform teams on GKE schedule distributed PyTorch training, vLLM inference and RL across both GPUs and TPUs from a single Kubernetes control plane.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: Mixed-accelerator fleets under one control plane commoditize the chip underneath and shift bargaining power toward cloud buyers.
insights.quote: across GPUs and TPUs on a single Kubernetes control plane

insights.claim: Anyscale and Google plan to extend the foundation to large-scale RL post-training frameworks and next-generation Ironwood (TPU v7x) slices on GKE.
insights.speaker: Lehui Liu
insights.so_what: RL post-training is flagged as the next battleground for accelerator share; watch Ironwood availability as a TPU demand catalyst.
insights.quote: stay tuned as we expand this foundation to large-scale RL post-training frameworks and next-generation Ironwood (TPU v7x) slices on GKE
